subtype: Faces are cues, not proof [Interpreting]
passage:
Nursing supervisor's note, medical ward, night shift.
Amandeep, our new staff nurse, is twenty-four and quick to learn. Tonight she came to me upset: the elderly man in bed 7 had scowled at her all evening, and she was sure he was angry with her for something. I asked what else she had noticed. She thought for a moment. He had been squinting at the clock. He hadn't touched his dinner. His voice was polite when he spoke. Together we went to his bed, and Amandeep asked gently, "Uncle, is anything bothering you?" He said his reading glasses were at home and the lights hurt his eyes, and his back ached from the bed. Not anger at all. Amandeep adjusted his pillows and dimmed the light over his bed, and his face relaxed. Afterwards she said, "I nearly avoided him all night." I told her a face is one clue; the words and the situation are the others.
— Salma

subtype: Faces are cues, not proof [Interpreting]
passage:
Thursday.
In today's budget meeting, when I explained why my project needed two more weeks, Bhupen grinned. A wide grin, right in the middle of my worst slide. I felt my face go hot. Was he mocking me? He's senior and I'm the new one; it would make sense. I spent the rest of the meeting half-listening, rehearsing a cold reply.
After the meeting I made myself go to his desk instead of stewing. "Bhupen, when I asked for the extra two weeks, you grinned. Did I say something funny?"
He looked horrified. "No! I grin when I'm nervous. I was worried the director would say no, and I was about to ask for the same thing for my team."
We ended up writing a joint request. The director approved both.
Note to self: a grin can be nerves, not a joke. Ask first. Fume later, if needed.
— Francis

qa.a: Two more weeks.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when Bhupen grinned?
qa.a: Francis felt embarrassed and hurt, face going hot, suspecting Bhupen was mocking.

qa.a: Francis asked Bhupen directly and calmly about the grin instead of stewing or replying coldly.

qa.a: He was nervous, worried the director would say no, because he was about to make the same request for his team.

Javier smiled, a real one this time. "Maybe I need a sister." "You can borrow me," she said. They walked out together, grumbling honestly about the seat man all the way to the bus.

You asked how the new customer support job is going. Honestly? The work is fine. It's the smiling that's tiring.

But last week I came home and snapped at Ma for asking if I'd eaten. I realised I'd been holding in eight hours of other people's anger.
So I've started walking home instead of taking the bus, and telling Ma about the worst call of the day. She listens and makes tea. I'm still smiling on calls. I'm just not only smiling any more.
Arnab

passage:

So he did, all day, even when a customer was rude, even when he was worried about his monthly target. By Friday his cheeks ached, and a customer asked, "Why are you grinning like that?"

Dear Ankita,
I've been at the Mumbai office for three weeks, and you told me yesterday that people think I'm a bit cold. I've been thinking about why.
I think it's the eyebrows. In the corridor or across the meeting room, when I see someone I know, I do what I've always done: a quick raise of the eyebrows and a small smile. At home in Goa, everyone does it. It means "hello, I see you, all good." But here I've noticed people say "Hi!" or "Good morning" out loud, or wave. Maybe they don't even notice my eyebrows. Maybe they think I'm ignoring them.
So I'm going to keep my eyebrow hello, because it's me, but add the words too. Starting tomorrow: eyebrows plus "Morning!"
Thank you for telling me honestly. I'd much rather know.
Maria

In team meetings, I've noticed your brows are often drawn together, a deep line between them. For a while I read it as unhappiness with the project, or with me as your team lead. Zubin

passage: Pranav, twenty-four, was on a client call with Singapore when a message from his mother flashed on his phone: Dadi had been taken to hospital. The call had ten minutes left, and he was presenting. His eyes filled. He blinked rapidly, squeezed them shut for a second, and looked up at the ceiling, trying to steady his voice. "As you can see on slide six..." His voice cracked. His colleague Tushar, sitting next to him, noticed the wet eyes and the phone. He leaned into the microphone. "Sorry, a quick technical pause. I'll take slide six." He muted Pranav's line and nodded at the door. Pranav stepped out, called his mother, and learned Dadi was stable. He breathed slowly in the corridor, washed his face, and came back for the last three minutes. After the call, Tushar said, "Go to the hospital. I'll send the summary."

qa.q: How long did the client call have left when Pranav saw the message?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he saw his mother's message?
qa.a: He was frightened and upset, his eyes filling as he tried to hold back tears and keep his voice steady.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that helped Pranav?
qa.a: He covered the slide, muted Pranav's line and signalled him to step out, giving him a short break.

qa.q: How did Tushar notice Pranav was struggling?
qa.a: He saw Pranav's wet eyes and the phone message, and heard his voice crack.

grounding: Shows a young professional blinking and squeezing his eyes to hold back tears on a call, and a short break helping more than pushing through.

subtype: Wet or squeezed eyes under pressure [Regulating]
passage: In the glass meeting room of the Delhi office, Hemant tore into Jasleen's campaign report in front of the whole team. "Sloppy. Did you even check the numbers?" Jasleen, twenty-five, felt her eyes sting. She looked up at the ceiling lights and blinked fast. Her throat was tight. She didn't want to cry in front of everyone, and she didn't want to argue while her voice shook. She took one breath and said, as evenly as she could, "I'd like to go through the numbers properly. Could I have five minutes to get the source sheet?" Hemant waved a hand. She walked to the washroom, let a few tears come, breathed slowly till her chest loosened, and washed her face. She came back with the sheet. Two of the numbers were his team's, not hers. Hemant looked at the sheet for a long time. "I'll check with my side," he said, quieter.

qa.q: How long a break did Jasleen ask for?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling during Hemant's criticism?
qa.a: She was hurt and upset, her eyes stinging and throat tight, and didn't want to cry or argue with a shaking voice.

qa.q: What made Jasleen's short break a wise choice?
qa.a: It let her release a few tears and calm her breathing privately, so she could come back steady with the evidence.

qa.q: How did Hemant respond after seeing the source sheet?
qa.a: He looked at it a long time and, more quietly, said he would check with his side, since two numbers were his team's.

grounding: Shows a young professional holding back tears by blinking and looking up, then taking a short break to breathe before continuing.

subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
passage: At the rural bank branch in Nalbari, Bhupen, twenty-five, sat across from Anand, a farmer, who had come to ask about the crop loan paperwork. Anand spoke haltingly, eyes on the table, as if expecting to be hurried. Bhupen leaned forward slightly and widened his eyes a little whenever Anand explained something: his flooded field, the seed costs, his daughter's school fees. It wasn't a stare; his eyes softened in between, and he nodded. "Go on," he said. Anand began to look up. He talked more easily, adding details he'd skipped at first. Bhupen took notes. Later, his colleague said, "You listen like it's the most interesting thing in the world." Bhupen shrugged. "It is, to him. And if I look bored, he stops talking, and I miss what he needs."

qa.q: What did Anand come to ask about?
qa.a: The crop loan paperwork.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he first started speaking?
qa.a: He seemed nervous and hesitant, speaking haltingly with his eyes down, as if expecting to be hurried.

qa.q: How did Bhupen's listening cues help?
qa.a: His slightly widened eyes, softening in between, and nods showed interest, so Anand looked up and shared more details.

qa.q: How did Bhupen's colleague see his listening?
qa.a: The colleague noticed he listened as if it were the most interesting thing in the world.

grounding: Shows a young professional widening the eyes naturally as a listening cue that encourages a speaker to say more.

subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
passage:
Dear Hrithik,
You asked me for feedback after your first two client interviews. The content was excellent. One small thing, though, as your mentor.
When clients speak, you open your eyes very wide and keep them that way, without blinking much, for their whole answer. I think you mean it to say "I'm interested." In the first interview it did. But by the second, the client started glancing away from you and cutting her answers short. A fixed wide stare can start to look strained, even a little alarming.
Try this: widen your eyes a little when something surprises or interests you, then let them relax. Nod. Look at your notes now and then. Interest comes across best when it moves with what's being said.
You're a natural listener. You don't need to prove it with your eyes.
Gautam

qa.q: How many client interviews had Hrithik done?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: What might the second client have been feeling during Hrithik's fixed stare?
qa.a: She may have felt uncomfortable or a little alarmed, glancing away and cutting her answers short.

qa.q: What does Gautam suggest Hrithik try?
qa.a: Widen the eyes slightly only at moments of interest, then relax, nod and glance at notes now and then.

qa.q: How does Gautam see Hrithik as a listener?
qa.a: Gautam sees Hrithik as a natural listener who doesn't need to prove interest with a fixed stare.

grounding: Shows a young professional's widened eyes working as a listening cue when natural but seeming strained when fixed.

subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
passage: Dhruv, you were my guest on episode one, so you'll enjoy this. I'm Chetan, twenty-six, and when I started this podcast, I read online that widening your eyes shows interest. So on video, I opened my eyes wide at everything my guests said. You were too polite to say it then. But when I watched the recording, I looked terrified. Like I'd seen a ghost behind you. My sister laughed so hard she cried. After that, I stopped performing. I listened, and let my face do what it wanted. When a guest said something that genuinely surprised me, my eyes widened on their own, for a second, and then relaxed. The guests started talking longer. One even said I was easy to open up to. So, Dhruv, honestly: sorry for staring at you like that. I promise my eyes are normal now. Mostly.

qa.q: What did Chetan read online about widening the eyes?
qa.a: That widening your eyes shows interest.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling on watching the first recording?
qa.a: Chetan felt embarrassed on seeing the terrified-looking stare, especially when Chetan's sister laughed so hard.

qa.q: What change made Chetan's listening cues work?
qa.a: Stopping the performance and letting the eyes widen naturally at real surprises, then relax.

qa.q: How did the later guests respond to Chetan's natural listening?
qa.a: They talked longer, and one said Chetan was easy to open up to.

grounding: Shows a young professional learning that widened eyes encourage a speaker only when natural, and a fixed wide look seems strained.

subtype: Gaze in cross-cultural teams [Mismatch]
passage: Lavanya beti, you're joining the team with the Helsinki office, so let your Dilnaz aunty tell you what I learnt. At twenty-four, I worked on a project with engineers from Finland and Brazil. On my first video meeting, the Brazilian lead, Marcos, looked straight at the camera the whole time. I found it intense, almost challenging, and kept looking down, as I did at home with seniors. Later my Finnish colleague Aino told me Marcos had asked if I was unhappy with the plan, because I never looked at him. I was shocked. I'd meant it as respect! Aino herself looked away often while thinking, and Marcos had thought she was bored too. We all laughed about it later. So we made a small rule: if you're unsure, ask. I learnt to meet Marcos's eyes more, and he learnt to give Aino her thinking pauses. Don't decide who someone is from their eyes, beti.

qa.q: Who told young Dilnaz that Marcos had asked about her?
qa.a: Her Finnish colleague Aino.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel when she heard Marcos thought she was unhappy?
qa.a: She was shocked, since she had looked down as a sign of respect, not unhappiness.

qa.q: What choice did the team make that helped?
qa.a: They agreed to ask when unsure, and each adapted: Dilnaz met Marcos's eyes more and Marcos allowed Aino her thinking pauses.

qa.q: How did Marcos read Dilnaz's lowered gaze?
qa.a: As possible unhappiness with the plan, because she never looked at him.

grounding: Shows a young professional learning that gaze norms differ in a cross-cultural team and that adapting and asking avoids stereotypes.

subtype: Gaze in cross-cultural teams [Mismatch]
passage: The video call with the Munich team kept freezing, and the product demo was due in thirty minutes. Ganga, twenty-five, was leading. Her colleague Deepak kept his eyes lowered whenever Stefan, the German manager, spoke to him directly. Stefan's voice got sharper. "Deepak, are you with us? You don't seem engaged." Deepak looked startled. Ganga knew Deepak's family had taught him that looking down while a senior speaks shows respect; he'd told her once. But on a frozen, pixelated screen, it just looked like he wasn't there. She unmuted. "Stefan, Deepak is very engaged; he wrote most of this code. I think with this bad connection, eye contact is hard to read. Deepak, could you walk us through the login fix?" Deepak looked into the camera and explained it clearly. Stefan nodded. "Very good. Thank you." After the call, Deepak said, "I'll try looking up more on video."

qa.q: How long was it until the product demo?
qa.a: Thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when Stefan asked if he was with them?
qa.a: He looked startled and was probably embarrassed, since he meant his lowered eyes as respect.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that bridged the misunderstanding?
qa.a: She explained Deepak's engagement and the hard-to-read connection, then invited him to present so his work showed.

qa.q: How did Stefan read Deepak's lowered eyes?
qa.a: As a sign Deepak wasn't engaged, not knowing it was meant as respect.

grounding: Shows a young professional bridging different gaze norms in a cross-cultural team call, adapting without stereotyping.

subtype: Gaze in cross-cultural teams [Mismatch]
passage: In the Bengaluru software office, Sonali, twenty-six, noticed that her new teammate Dolma never looked the manager, Mr Pieter, in the eye during stand-ups. Pieter, who had moved from Amsterdam, liked people to hold his gaze. After a week, he said to Sonali, "Is Dolma unhappy here? She won't look at me." Sonali didn't want to guess or explain for Dolma. At lunch she asked Dolma, casually, "How are you finding Pieter?" Dolma smiled. "He's nice. But he stares so much! In my family, looking straight at a senior feels rude. I look down to be polite." Sonali laughed. "He thinks you're unhappy." Dolma's eyes widened. "Oh no." Sonali suggested she tell Pieter herself. The next day Dolma did, and Pieter laughed too. "I'll stop staring so hard. And you look up now and then?" "Deal," Dolma said. Both adjusted a little.

qa.q: Where had Mr Pieter moved from?
qa.a: From Amsterdam.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she learned Pieter thought she was unhappy?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little dismayed, her eyes widening, since she had meant to be polite.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that avoided a stereotype?
qa.a: Sonali asked Dolma directly instead of guessing or explaining for her, and suggested Dolma tell Pieter herself.

qa.q: How did Pieter respond once Dolma explained?
qa.a: He laughed, agreed to stop staring so hard, and asked her to look up now and then.

grounding: Shows young professionals learning that gaze norms differ and adapting with curiosity rather than assumptions.

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday night.
Gave my first big presentation to the regional managers today. Five minutes in, I saw Anjali, the operations lead, look down at her phone. Then again. Then she typed something. My stomach dropped. I'd spent a week on those slides. I kept going, but my voice got faster and flatter.
Afterwards, I almost walked past her. But I made myself ask. "Anjali, I noticed you on your phone. Was the presentation losing you?"
She looked surprised. "No! I was forwarding your cost slide to the Nagpur team in real time. They've been asking for exactly that." She showed me the message.
I felt stupid. And relieved.
She did add, "I should have said so. Next time, tell me if it bothers you." So I will.
— Divyansh

qa.q: What was Anjali forwarding to the Nagpur team?
qa.a: The cost slide.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when Anjali looked at her phone?
qa.a: Divyansh felt a sinking disappointment, stomach dropping, worried the presentation was losing her, and sped up nervously.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that was kinder than assuming disrespect?
qa.a: Divyansh asked Anjali directly about the phone instead of walking past her.

qa.q: How did Anjali see her own phone use?
qa.a: As doing a real work task, forwarding the slide, though she admitted she should have said so.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading a colleague's phone use as boredom when it was a work task, and checking kindly.

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage:
Kiran: hey, can I say something about today's meeting?
Tushar: sure
Kiran: you were on your phone most of the time I was explaining the vendor issue. I couldn't tell if you were bored or dealing with something
Tushar: ah. sorry. it was the warehouse, a truck got stuck and they kept messaging me
Kiran: that makes sense. it just felt like I was talking to a wall 😅
Tushar: fair. I should've said "one sec, emergency" instead of just typing
Kiran: yeah that would've helped. also, next week's vendor meeting is really important. can we both keep phones face down unless it's urgent?
Tushar: deal. and if it's urgent I'll step out
Kiran: perfect 🙂
Tushar: thanks for telling me instead of stewing

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Kiran felt frustrated and unsure, as if talking to a wall, not knowing if Tushar was bored or busy.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that was kind and clear?
qa.a: Kiran named the concern without blame, asked what was happening, and requested full attention for the next important meeting.

qa.q: How did Tushar see the phone use once Kiran raised it?

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage: At the monthly meeting of the milk cooperative in Anand district, Santosh, twenty-five, was explaining the new collection timings to the committee. Parveen, the secretary, kept glancing at her phone, thumb moving fast. Two members exchanged looks. Santosh felt irritation rise. He had worked hard on this plan. Was she even listening? He paused and said, calmly, "Parveen-ji, I notice you're on your phone. Is something urgent? This part needs your approval." Parveen looked up, apologetic. "Sorry, Santosh-bhai. The tanker driver is stuck at the bridge with today's milk. I was arranging another route." Santosh's irritation melted. "Then please sort that first. We'll wait five minutes." She made one more call, put the phone face down and said, "Now, the timings. Go ahead." She approved them with one change. Afterwards a committee member said, "Good that you asked. I thought she didn't care."

qa.q: Where was the tanker driver stuck?
qa.a: At the bridge, with today's milk.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when Parveen kept looking at her phone?
qa.a: He felt irritated and a bit hurt, wondering if she was even listening to the plan he had worked hard on.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that was kinder than assuming disrespect?
qa.a: He named what he noticed calmly, asked if something was urgent, and then gave her time to sort it before continuing.

qa.q: How did the committee member see Parveen's phone use before Santosh asked?
qa.a: The member thought Parveen didn't care about the meeting.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing a colleague's phone glances, naming the concern and asking instead of assuming disrespect.
